strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: treating VR sketches as temporally ordered sequences of strokes and points, rather than unordered point clouds, is a meaningful and underexplored angle. The 'order matters' hypothesis is directly tested and supported.

Strong dataset contribution: VRSKETCH2SHAPE is the first open-access, multi-category VR sketch dataset (4 categories, ~20.8k synthetic + 900 real sketch-shape pairs), addressing the data-scarcity problem in this domain. The surface-snapping mechanism for real data collection is a sensible design that measurably reduces sketch-to-shape Chamfer distance (5.5 vs 55.6 for 3DVRChair).

Ablations directly support the central claim: removing stroke/point ordering drops F-score from 56.8 to 48.9 and increases CD from 5.1 to 7.1; alternative representations (point clouds, rendered images) degrade further (Table 3). This isolates the contribution of order-aware encoding from the diffusion generator.

Broad empirical study: zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation (Fig. 5), cross-modal shape completion from partial sketches (Fig. 7), and quantitative comparisons on both 3DVRChair and the proposed dataset show large gains (e.g., ~60% CD reduction, >40% F-score improvement over Luo et al.).

Reproducibility: implementation details (Fourier feature count, embedding dim, BERT depth, optimizer, batch sizes, training schedule) are provided, and the authors commit to open-sourcing data and models.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited to four relatively simple/symmetric categories (chair, table, cabinet, airplane). It is unclear whether the order-aware benefit generalizes to more complex, organic, or articulated shapes where stroke topology is less regular and the heuristic stroke-ordering assumption may break down.

The synthetic sketch generation pipeline is a hand-crafted heuristic (saliency sub-sampling, Bézier fitting, DFS-based endpoint traversal with 10% stochastic skip). The claim that these synthetic sequences provide 'effective supervision for real-world generalization' is supported only indirectly; the ordering heuristic may not match human drawing order, and no analysis quantifies the distributional gap between synthetic and real stroke orderings.

Baseline coverage is thin: only Luo et al. has released code/weights, and the 2D LAS-Diffusion baseline is a retrained adaptation rather than the original method, so the comparison may not fully reflect the state of the art (e.g., no comparison with more recent VR/sketch-based generators).

The real dataset is modest (900 sketches from 15 participants, ~225 person-hours), which limits statistical strength of the few-shot and generalization claims, and the 400-pair real evaluation set is small.

Reconstruction fidelity is bounded by a frozen 3D VQ-VAE and 64^3 SDF resolution, which the authors acknowledge; this constrains fine geometric detail and could confound the comparison of order-aware vs. order-free variants if the bottleneck dominates.

Some claims (e.g., 'first framework,' 'state-of-the-art') are stated strongly relative to the limited set of directly comparable baselines; the paper would benefit from clearer scoping and a failure-case discussion.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: the paper is the first to explicitly model the temporal order of VR strokes, whereas prior VR sketch-to-shape methods (e.g., Luo et al., Chen et al.) discard stroke order by treating sketches as unordered point clouds. The framing is supported by a clean ablation (w/o ordering: F-score 48.9 vs. 56.8, CD 7.1 vs. 5.1), so the central claim is not merely asserted.

Multi-part, reusable contribution: (i) a learning-free synthetic sketch pipeline (surface sampling -> SES salient points -> EMAP Bezier fitting -> culling -> connectivity-graph DFS ordering) that produces 20,838 paired samples in ~10 hours, (ii) 900 real hand-drawn VR sketches across four categories with stroke and point ordering, collected via a surface-snapping Unity interface, and (iii) the order-aware encoder + SDFusion model. Table 1 documents the dataset's scale and alignment advantage (asymmetric sketch-to-shape CD 5.5 vs. 55.6 for 3DVRChair), and the authors commit to open-sourcing data and models.

Strong, consistent empirical results across both an existing public benchmark and the new dataset: on 3DVRChair the method reaches F-score 31.1 / CD 25.8 vs. 26.6 / 35.5 for Luo et al. and 26.1 / 66.0 for the 2D LAS-Diffusion variant; on VRSKETCH2SHAPE it reaches 69.8 F / 4.8 CD vs. 48.8 / 13.0 across all categories. The evaluation protocol (bounding-box alignment, bidirectional CD, F-score at delta=0.02) follows prior practice, making the comparison legible.

Thorough analysis beyond headline numbers: zero-shot synthetic-to-real evaluation, a few-shot adaptation curve (Fig. 5), order-aware partial-sketch completion (Fig. 6-7), generation speed (6.61 s on an RTX 4090, ~50 h training), and ablations over ordering, augmentation, synthetic pretraining, encoder choice, and sketch format (point-cloud and rendered-image variants at 30.8 / 25.8 and 23.8 / 62.6). These jointly argue that the gains come from the sequential formulation and synthetic supervision, not just the diffusion backbone.

Good reproducibility: concrete architecture details (L=10 Fourier bands, D=256, 2-layer MLP, 6 transformer layers, 8 heads), optimizer settings (AdamW, 1e-4, ReduceLROnPlateau), batch sizes, 200/300 epoch schedules, 100 DDIM steps, and evaluation thresholds are all reported, which is unusual for a paper of this scope.
weaknesses: Narrow external baseline set. Only Luo et al. [35] and a re-implemented 2D LAS-Diffusion variant are compared. The paper itself notes that other recent sketch-to-3D methods (Deep3DSketch+ [6], Sketch2Model [70], Chen et al.) could not be evaluated due to missing code/checkpoints, so the 'outperforms prior work by a large margin' claim rests on a thin set of competitors, and the tuning budget / hyperparameter search applied to the retrained baselines is not documented.

The paper's headline claim ('Order Matters') is not tested with the most direct control. The w/o-ordering ablation removes both stroke/point index embeddings and, with them, stroke segmentation, so it conflates temporal order with stroke grouping. A variant that retains stroke structure but shuffles stroke order (at training or inference) is the experiment that would isolate temporal ordering; the point-cloud ablation (30.8/25.8) partially covers this but does not fully decouple the two factors. This is a readily fixable but currently material gap in evidence for the paper's central thesis.

Potential train/test distribution match inflating gains on VRSKETCH2SHAPE. The synthetic test sketches are produced by the same heuristic pipeline used for pretraining, so the very large margins on the authors' own dataset (CD 4.0 vs. 13.4 for chair-only) may partly reflect matched distributions rather than a strictly better model. The comparison on the independent 3DVRChair benchmark is noticeably more modest (F 31.1 vs. 26.6), and the authors do not analyze or quantify this discrepancy.

The real-sketch benchmark is made easier by surface snapping, and the consequences are not analyzed. Table 1 shows snapping reduces sketch-shape misalignment from 55.6 to 5.5 CD, i.e., the collected 'real' sketches are far cleaner than unconstrained freehand VR sketches (as in 3DVRChair). It is unclear how much of the reported synthetic-to-real generalization reflects genuine robustness versus the eased benchmark; an evaluation on unsnapped or deliberately noisy sketches would be informative.

Output fidelity is bounded by an external frozen representation. The 64^3 VQ-VAE/SDFusion latent caps fine-grained detail, and the authors acknowledge that reconstructions appear 'slightly oversmooth.' This qualifies the 'high-fidelity' framing: the geometric ceiling is set by a pretrained decoder, not by the proposed model, and no end-to-end or higher-resolution variant is demonstrated.

Limited object coverage and no usability evidence. Evaluation spans four categories (chair, table, cabinet, airplane) of relatively simple ShapeNet shapes; generalization to articulated, thin-shell, or topologically complex objects is untested. Given the motivation of accelerating rapid ideation, a user study or at least an interactive-workflow demonstration would strengthen the practical claim, but none is provided.

No variance or significance reporting. Metrics appear to be single-run without seeds, error bars, or confidence intervals (e.g., the Fig. 5 adaptation curves have none), which matters for ablations whose margins are small (augmentation vs. ordering: 49.0 vs. 48.9 F-score, 6.6 vs. 7.1 CD).

Minor presentation and validation issues: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('will be released open-source on'), naming is inconsistent ('SketchBert' vs. 'SketchBERT'), and the Table 1 caption's description of the asymmetric Chamfer distance is ambiguous. More substantively, the DFS-based stroke ordering is claimed to 'approximate human drawing order' but is never quantitatively validated against the ordering statistics of the 900 collected real sketches, which would be a natural and cheap check.

strengths: Introduces the first multi-category open-access dataset for sequential VR sketches, combining 20,838 synthetic and 900 real sketch-shape pairs across four categories (Table 1).
The synthetic sketch generation pipeline is scalable and provides large-scale paired supervision; real data collection involved 15 participants and roughly 225 person-hours (Sec. 3.1).
The order-aware BERT-style encoder coupled with SDFusion achieves strong quantitative gains over baselines on both 3DVRChair and the proposed dataset (Table 2).
Ablations systematically test stroke ordering, augmentations, pretraining, and sketch format, showing that order embeddings and synthetic pretraining contribute to performance (Table 3).

The paper includes partial-sketch completion and few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation experiments (Figs. 5-7), and provides relatively detailed training/inference settings and an open-source release plan.
weaknesses: The core evaluation is compromised by surface snapping: real test sketches are projected onto the ground-truth 3D model during collection (Sec. 3.1), so the inputs are effectively sparse surface samples of the target geometry. The sketch-to-shape CD of 5.5 vs. 55.6 for 3DVRChair (Table 1) confirms that the proposed benchmark is far easier and leaks target-shape information, making the claimed 'shape generation from VR sketches' task closer to surface reconstruction from a traced reference mesh.

The comparison with prior work may be unfair if baselines consume raw VR sketches while the proposed model is evaluated on snapped sketches. The paper does not report raw, unsnapped sketch results from its own dataset, so real-world generalization to natural VR sketching is unproven.

It is not specified whether the 20,838 synthetic training pairs are shape-disjoint from the 400 real evaluation sketches. If the same ShapeNet shapes are used, the zero-shot synthetic-to-real claim is invalid and the large 'w/o pretraining' collapse (Table 3) could be partly explained by shape leakage rather than pure synthetic supervision.

The synthetic pipeline is described as 'learning-free' and 'entirely training-free' (Fig. 1, Sec. 2.3), yet it uses EMAP [22], a neural edge reconstruction method, and possibly other learned sampling components. This contradicts the stated claim and should be corrected or clarified.

The 'order matters' claim is not fully isolated. The ablation removes stroke/point order embeddings, but does not compare true human drawing order against shuffled or randomized orders. The synthetic stroke ordering via a proximity DFS is heuristic and not validated against human sequential drawing behavior; performance without order remains substantial (48.9 F-score), so order is beneficial but not clearly the dominant factor.

The mechanism for conditioning SDFusion on the variable-length BERT token sequence is underspecified. The paper does not explain how the sequence embeddings are integrated into the diffusion model (e.g., cross-attention, pooled conditioning), limiting reproducibility and architectural understanding.
Only two baselines are evaluated, and recent VR sketch-based methods are either omitted or not compared under a common protocol. This weakens the evidence for the claimed superiority.

There are minor citation/formatting issues, including confusion between references [34] and [35] in Sec. 5.2 and an incomplete abstract sentence ('will be released open-source on'), which reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and under-explored problem — 3D shape generation from sequential VR sketches — and correctly identifies temporal stroke/point order as information that prior point-cloud-based VR pipelines discard.

Substantial, open resource contribution: a multi-category dataset (4 categories) with 20,838 synthetic + 900 real sketch–shape pairs that preserves both stroke order and within-stroke point order, together with a fully learning-free synthetic generation pipeline (surface sampling → saliency sub-sampling → spline fitting → culling → DFS ordering) that produces 20k samples in ~10 hours and is shown to be effective supervision for real data.

Large, consistent quantitative gains over the strongest available VR baseline on both benchmarks: on 3DVRChair CD 25.8 vs 35.5 and F-score 31.1 vs 26.6; on VRSketch2Shape all-categories F-score 69.8 vs 48.8 and CD 4.8 vs 13.0, with a retrained LAS-Diffusion also clearly outperformed.

Unusually thorough empirical study for this type of paper: zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation, participant-based user study (38 raters, 1,900 ratings), free-hand (no-reference) sketch generalization, unseen-category evaluation, partial-sketch completion, DDIM step/accuracy tradeoff, and ablations over ordering, augmentations, pretraining, encoder design, and sketch format (point cloud vs multi-view images).

Ablations are informative and partly falsifiable, e.g. removing stroke/point indices (48.9 vs 56.8 F-score), removing synthetic pretraining (12.0 F-score), and alternative sketch formats (30.8 point cloud, 23.8 images) directly support the design choices.

Honest reporting of limitations and mixed evidence: the supplement openly reports that reversing stroke order barely hurts (56.2 vs 56.8), that BFS-ordered sketches degrade performance, and that unseen classes (truck, bed, toilet) are sometimes reconstructed with table/chair-like priors; the claim is accordingly reframed around consistent sequential structure rather than human-like order.

Good reproducibility: explicit architecture hyperparameters (L=10 Fourier bands, D=256, 6-layer/8-head transformer), optimizer settings, training schedules, hardware (RTX 4090), per-stage timings, and a stated intent to release data, code, and models.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the model is essentially a BERT-style tokenizer over ordered strokes with Fourier positional/point features conditioning the existing SDFusion latent diffusion model and a frozen 3D VQ-VAE. The individual components (BERT, SDFusion, VQ-VAE, Fourier features) are off-the-shelf; the novelty rests mainly on the tokenization scheme and the dataset.

The real-data benchmark is made substantially easier by the surface-snapping mechanism used during data collection: real sketches are projected onto the reference 3D shape, removing exactly the depth ambiguity and geometric misalignment that the paper itself identifies as the core VR sketching challenge. All headline quantitative results (Tables 2–4) are on snapped sketches; the unsnapped evaluation (Sec. A-3) and free-hand generalization (Fig. 6, A-4) are reported qualitatively or in a small user study, so the reported real-data accuracy is likely optimistic relative to genuine in-the-wild VR sketching.

The participant split is not specified. 15 participants produced 900 sketches, of which 500 are used for fine-tuning and 400 for evaluation; if the evaluation sketches are not drawn by held-out participants, subject-specific drawing-style leakage could inflate the reported synthetic-to-real generalization. This is a potentially serious confound that should be reported.

The 'order matters' thesis is only partially supported by the authors' own ablations: reversing stroke order changes F-score by only 0.6 (56.2 vs 56.8) and scrambling strokes only drops to 54.6, while the large drop in 'w/o ordering' (48.9) comes from deleting stroke/point index embeddings entirely — i.e. removing stroke identity rather than temporal order. Likewise, the large BFS-vs-DFS gap (47.8 vs 56.8) plausibly reflects matching the synthetic DFS ordering heuristic rather than a genuine human temporal prior. The title/framing overstates the strength of the temporal-order claim relative to the evidence.

Baseline breadth is limited: only Luo et al. [42] (plus a re-trained LAS-Diffusion) is compared quantitatively, despite several related recent 3D-sketch-to-shape works (e.g. Deep3DSketch+ [8], VRKSketch2Gaussian [18], Sketch2Mesh [19], 3Doodle [14]) being discussed. The re-trained LAS-Diffusion baseline may also not have been tuned under a comparable budget, making that comparison somewhat weak.

Statistical rigor is thin: 100 real test pairs per category, no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on the main comparisons, and the user study rests on a single cohort of 38 raters. It is difficult to judge whether the reported margins (e.g. 64.3 vs 42.2 F-score on the chair subset) are stable across splits.

Absolute reconstruction fidelity remains coarse and over-smoothed (e.g. Fig. 4, A-6), which the authors correctly attribute to the frozen 64^3 SDF VQ-VAE decoder; this limits the practical utility of the outputs for the design workflows the paper motivates, and end-to-end or higher-resolution training is left entirely to future work.

Some evaluation details are ambiguous or inconsistent across tables: Table 4's ablation numbers (chair subset, zero-shot) differ substantially in scale from Table 2's all-category numbers, and Table 1's CD statistic (5.5) uses a different, asymmetric sketch-to-shape measure than the symmetric generation metric; the text's '60% CD reduction / 40% F-score improvement' applies only to the authors' own dataset and is not flagged clearly enough.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and under-explored problem: 3D shape generation from sequential VR sketches, where prior work (e.g., Luo et al.) discards stroke/point order by treating sketches as unordered point clouds. The observation that VR sketching inherently carries temporal/structural cues is compelling and practically relevant.

Substantial dataset contribution: the first open-source, multi-category VR sketch dataset with explicit stroke order and point order annotations, combining 20,838 synthetic pairs with 900 real hand-drawn sketches across four categories, plus a documented surface-snapping VR interface. This directly addresses the data-scarcity problem (3DVRChair has only 1,005 chair-only pairs) and is likely to be widely used.

Strong and consistent quantitative gains: on 3DVRChair the method improves F-score from 26.6 to 31.1 and reduces CD from 35.5 to 25.8; on their own dataset the improvements are larger (e.g., 64.3 vs 42.2 F-score on chairs). Notably, they retrain the LAS-Diffusion baseline on their full synthetic dataset for a fair comparison rather than relying on published numbers.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a generation paper: zero-shot synthetic-to-real transfer, few-shot adaptation curves, a 38-participant user study with 1,900 ratings, ablations on ordering/augmentation/pretraining/encoder/format, partial-sketch completion, non-snapped and free-hand sketches, unseen categories, sketcher-expertise effects, and a speed/accuracy tradeoff. This breadth materially strengthens the claims.

The learning-free synthetic sketch pipeline demonstrably provides effective supervision: the model generalizes to real sketches with little or no fine-tuning, and the w/o-pretraining ablation (F-score collapses from 56.8 to 12.0) isolates the value of the synthetic data.

The ablation on sketch format (point clouds: 30.8 F-score; rendered images: 23.8) convincingly shows that the sequential point–stroke formulation, not just the diffusion backbone, drives much of the improvement, and the SketchBERT-encoder ablation (50.4) supports the encoder design choice.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest. The architecture is essentially a 3D-adapted BERT encoder (the authors acknowledge its similarity to SketchBERT) coupled to an off-the-shelf SDFusion model with a frozen 3D VQ-VAE. The core technical contribution is the conditioning interface and embedding scheme rather than a fundamentally new generative or representation-learning approach.

The title/claim 'Order Matters' is stronger than the authors' own evidence. Table A-1 shows Reverse Order (56.2 F) is essentially on par with the best model (56.8 F), and the supplementary correctly concedes it is 'consistent sequential structure' rather than human-like ordering that matters. The headline framing should be softened accordingly, since the sharpest order-aware-vs-order-agnostic gap is only about +6.6 F-score in the partial-sketch setting.

Generation quality is bounded by the frozen 3D VQ-VAE at 64^3 resolution, producing noticeably coarse/oversmooth geometry; the authors acknowledge this, but it limits fine-grained fidelity and is a real ceiling on the practical value of the outputs.

Failure modes on unseen categories are significant and only partially mitigated: in Fig. A-5, trucks and beds collapse into table-like structures, indicating heavy reliance on learned category priors rather than a purely sketch-driven mapping. The claim of 'robust sketch-to-shape mapping' is therefore overstated for out-of-distribution inputs.

The real data remains limited (900 sketches, 4 categories; 400-pair evaluation set). The synthetic sketches dominate training, and the heuristic generator (saliency sampling, Bézier fitting, culling, DFS ordering) may not match the distribution of natural human sketching; the strong synthetic-to-real transfer partly reflects the alignment of the synthetic data with the surface-snapped real sketches.

Baseline coverage is thin. Beyond Luo et al. and a retrained LAS-Diffusion, no other recent VR/sketch-to-shape methods are compared (Chen et al. is excluded due to unavailable code). This makes the 'outperforms prior work by a large margin' claim rest on a small comparison set.

Presentation issues: the abstract is truncated ('released open-source on'), and there are minor formatting inconsistencies. More substantively, the paper does not report variance/error bars on the main quantitative results, and the evaluation relies on geometry-only metrics (CD/F-score) that do not capture topological correctness, making the user study the main evidence for structural fidelity.

strengths: Provides an open-source VR sketch dataset with 900 real hand-drawn sketches across four categories plus ~20.8k synthetic sketch–shape pairs, with stroke and point ordering explicitly preserved. This addresses a real gap, since the only other public VR-sketch benchmark (3DVRChair) contains 1,005 chair-only pairs.

The surface-snapping VR interface is a sensible data-collection design that removes depth ambiguity, and Table 1 shows the resulting sketches are far better aligned to their target shapes than prior VR sketch data (CD 5.5 vs 55.6), yielding cleaner supervision and evaluation.

The order-aware encoder is well specified: two-level (stroke index and within-stroke point index) sequence embeddings, spatial Fourier features for coordinates, learned SEP/EOS tokens, and sketch-specific augmentations (stroke/point dropping, stroke swapping), trained end-to-end against a frozen latent diffusion generator in a single stage.

The experimental suite is broad for a paper of this length: two datasets, zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation, component ablations, a user study, free-hand sketches, unseen categories, partial-sketch inputs, DDIM-step speed/accuracy tradeoff, and wall-clock generation speed.

Large and consistent empirical margins over the strongest publicly available baseline (Luo et al.) on both 3DVRChair and the proposed dataset, supported by a 38-participant user study with a clear advantage on both reference-guided (3.92 vs 2.76) and free-hand (3.60 vs 2.02) sketches.

The paper is candid about limitations (frozen 64^3 VQ-VAE bounding fidelity and causing oversmoothing) and about failure modes (truck/bed sketches reconstructed as tables in the unseen-class experiment).
Writing is clear, implementation details (optimizer, learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, dropout, encoder dimensions) are reported, and code/data are promised as open source.
weaknesses: The paper's central thesis is contradicted by the authors' own evidence. Table A-1 shows that reversing stroke order yields F-score 56.2 / CD 5.0, which is indistinguishable from the full model (56.8 / 5.1) and on CD is actually better; scrambled strokes only fall to 54.6. The one large drop comes from removing stroke and point index embeddings entirely (48.9 / 7.1), which deletes all positional information and renders the transformer permutation-invariant over the token bag rather than ablating temporal order. The ablation therefore does not isolate ordering, and the supportable claim collapses to the much weaker and less novel statement that positional encodings plus stroke grouping help. This is a material issue with the title and the framing, and the appendix 'reframing' does not repair the main paper.

The proposed benchmark's validity is questionable. Because real sketches are surface-snapped onto the target mesh, the model input is essentially a sparse set of ground-truth surface points with connectivity. Table 1 reports a sketch-to-shape CD of 5.5 for this dataset, which is comparable to (indeed larger than) the model's reported output CD of 4.0 on the same data; the quantitative task is thus close to surface reconstruction from GT-sampled points rather than sketch-to-shape from genuine free-hand drawing. This plausibly inflates the large gap to Luo et al. (13.0) and undercuts claims of practical value for early-stage ideation.

Baseline coverage is thin for the claim that the method 'outperforms prior work by a large margin.' Only Luo et al. is a true like-for-like comparison; the LAS-Diffusion variant consumes 2D renders and is not an equivalent input modality, and Chen et al. is excluded for lack of released code. Other VR-sketch-to-shape methods (e.g., VRSS / VRsketch2Gaussian, both cited) are not compared, and the re-trained baseline's training/evaluation fairness on the authors' own dataset is not established.

Possible shape-level overlap between synthetic training data and real evaluation data is not addressed. Participants sketched 'multiple objects from ShapeNet' and the synthetic pipeline generates sketches from meshes (Fig. 2 shows a ShapeNet chair), yet the paper never states that the synthetic training shapes are disjoint from the real evaluation shapes. If they overlap, the zero-shot synthetic-to-real numbers could be driven by memorized shape priors rather than learned sketch-to-geometry mapping; the unseen-class failures reported in Sec. A-5 (trucks and beds reconstructed as table-like structures) are consistent with substantial prior reliance and make this clarification necessary.

Free-hand sketching — the setting that matters most for the stated application — is evaluated only qualitatively (Figs. 6 and A-4) plus a small user study (40 sketches, 38 participants). No CD/F-score is reported on free-hand or unsnapped sketches, so the robustness-to-domain-shift claim is not quantitatively substantiated. Similarly, the 'partial sketch / cross-modal completion' capability is largely in-distribution: the model is trained with 15% stroke dropping and 30% point dropping and inference pads with learned MASK tokens, and the quantitative completion curve (Fig. A-1) is computed on the same snapped distribution.

The dataset is narrow for a 'multi-category' benchmark: 900 real sketches from 15 participants across four categories (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes), all drawn with a reference model, totaling roughly 225 person-hours. No inter-annotator variability, sketch-complexity statistics (strokes/points per sketch), or category-diversity analysis is provided, and generalization claims beyond furniture/airplane are weakly supported.

The reconstruction ceiling is set by a component the paper does not train: a frozen 64^3 3D VQ-VAE. The authors acknowledge this bounds fine-grained geometric detail and yields oversmooth outputs, which is visible in the qualitative comparisons. For a paper whose title promises structural fidelity from sketch structure, this is a significant architectural constraint rather than a minor limitation.

Headline comparisons in Table 2 lack error bars or significance testing, and the main benchmark is designed, annotated, and evaluated by the authors, with the sole strong baseline re-trained by them; the resulting very large margins (e.g., F-score 69.8 vs 48.8) therefore need independent validation before they can be treated as evidence of a fundamental advance.

Presentation defects: the abstract is truncated mid-sentence ('released open-source on .'), Table 2 mixes a non-comparable 2D-render baseline with like-for-like results under only an asterisk, and the main text does not report the stroke/point statistics that would be needed to judge whether the order-aware encoder is actually exploiting temporal structure.
